newsitem.title: UK: Sick building syndrome is a myth, architect says.
newsitem.headline: Sick building syndrome is a myth, architect says.

text.p: Sick building syndrome, the idea that poor air conditioning, harsh lighting or uncomfortable desks are to blame for colds and other ailments, is a myth, a British architect said on Friday.
Alexi Marmot said the syndrome was more likely to be caused by bad management and low job satisfaction than a poor working environment.
"I wouldn't use the term sick building syndrome (SBS) at all," Marmot told the annual conference of the Royal College of Psychiatrists.
"There are sick organisations and poor management and a lot of people who have difficult lives -- and that is what we are seeing here," she said.
Marmot and her husband, epidemiology professor Sir Michael Marmot, are leading a major study of the health of 6,800 London civil servants.

She surveyed 44 office buildings in which 4,100 people worked and found that the symptoms of the syndrome -- which also include a sore throat, headache, tiredness and coughs -- were linked to passive smoking, lengthy commuting and housing problems.
Workers said good air conditioning was important and that working at a computer screen for more than 20 hours a week increased their symptoms.
But she also found that people with little support at work had many SBS symptoms, while those whose work was less demanding had fewer.

"Environment is important in terms of comfort and well-being but as far as sick building syndrome and these symptoms causing people to take days off work, our work suggests that that is a spurious association," Marmot said.
She said there was a large body of evidence that sealed buildings caused SBS. But when the symptoms were put into a wider psycho-social context, the evidence did not hold up, Marmot argued.
"Frankly, apart from some extreme examples, physical things play almost no part in sick building syndrome," she said.
